title: Thanksgiving History from Wampanoag Perspectives
summary: Read Wampanoag accounts, a 1621 eyewitness record, and two historical images. Trace how the harvest gathering became part of the Thanksgiving story and why some Indigenous people observe a National Day of Mourning.
intro: Wampanoag people had their own communities, diplomacy, and traditions of giving thanks long before English settlers arrived. The 1621 harvest gathering at Patuxet, now Plymouth, is one moment in that longer history. Wampanoag historians and community members help us see what the familiar holiday story leaves out.

paragraphs.text: Patuxet was a Wampanoag village. Long before the English founded Plymouth there in 1620, Wampanoag people had seasonal harvest gatherings and daily practices of giving thanks. They also had decades of experience with European traders and explorers. In 1614 Thomas Hunt kidnapped Tisquantum and other Wampanoag men. When Tisquantum returned in 1619, he found that an epidemic had killed most of his home community.

The engraved map below was published in 1616, before the Mayflower arrived. It labels the coast using English names, including “Plimouth.” Read the map alongside the Wampanoag history of Patuxet and ask whose names the map records.

sections.heading: The 1621 gathering and the alliance behind it

paragraphs.text: In spring 1621, Wampanoag sachem Ousamequin, called Massasoit in many English accounts, and Plymouth governor John Carver agreed to mutual protection. Diplomacy gave Ousamequin a way to respond to an unfamiliar settlement in Wampanoag country. The written terms survive in English, and the museum notes that how they were translated remains uncertain.

In the fall, Edward Winslow described Ousamequin arriving with about ninety men. He recorded three days of gathering and that Wampanoag men brought five deer. His brief account gives no detailed menu or guest list. Wampanoag historian Paula Peters points out how English-written records often leave Wampanoag women out of view. The surviving account tells us far less about Native participants’ experiences than many later retellings suggest.

sections.heading: How the gathering became a national story

paragraphs.text: Relations deteriorated as English settlements expanded and conflicts grew over land and colonial law. Ousamequin’s son Metacom later built alliances to defend Native homelands, and war began in 1675. Centuries later, during the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national Thanksgiving in 1863. Congress established the fourth Thursday of November as the federal holiday in 1941.

In her 1914 painting, Jennie Augusta Brownscombe puts a settler leading a prayer at the center and places several figures meant to represent Wampanoag participants along the edges of the scene. Compare that arrangement with Winslow’s account of Ousamequin, his large party, and their contribution of deer. The painting shows how a twentieth-century artist imagined the event almost three centuries later.

In 1970, anniversary organizers invited Wamsutta (Frank James), an Aquinnah Wampanoag man, to speak. He wrote about dispossession and Wampanoag survival. When organizers offered him a replacement speech, he declined to read it. That year Native people and supporters gathered at Cole’s Hill in Plymouth for the first National Day of Mourning. Read his speech and the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe’s account together.

Indigenous people hold different views about the holiday. Some gather with family or give thanks, some observe the National Day of Mourning, and some do both. The Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe’s own cultural resources offer a starting point for learning about the community today.

questions: What does Winslow record about the Wampanoag contribution to the gathering? What questions does his account leave unanswered?
Whose names are visible on the 1616 map? How does that choice shape the story the map tells?
Compare Brownscombe’s painting and Wamsutta’s speech. What does each work ask its audience to remember?
